title: The US Judge Handling Adani's Case Just Told Prosecutors Their Explanation Wasn't Good Enough
excerpt: Judge Nicholas Garaufis refused to dismiss criminal charges against Gautam Adani outright, ordering the Justice Department to justify dropping the case by July 13.
body:
A US federal judge has refused to rubber-stamp the dismissal of criminal charges against Gautam Adani, ordering prosecutors to come back and explain themselves before he will consider letting the case go.

Brooklyn-based US District Judge Nicholas Garaufis ruled on Friday that the Justice Department's announcement in May that it would no longer pursue the prosecution was "terse, bland and conclusory" — and did not give the court enough to work with.

"The government's terse, bland and conclusory statement affords the court neither a sufficient basis to reach any conclusion, nor the opportunity to conduct any analysis of the government's request for dismissal," Garaufis wrote, giving the DOJ until July 13 to submit a fuller justification.

## The Charges and Their Politics

Adani was indicted in November 2024, at the tail end of the Biden administration, on allegations that he agreed to bribe Indian government officials so an Adani Group subsidiary could win approval to develop a solar energy project, and then misled American investors about the company's anti-corruption practices.

The decision to drop the case came during Donald Trump's second term, making it the latest in a string of high-profile white-collar prosecutions that the Justice Department has sought to end under the current administration. Legal experts note that the timing and pattern have raised questions about the independence of prosecutorial decisions — though they also acknowledge that US judges have very limited power to force prosecutors to continue cases they no longer wish to pursue.

## Adani's Defence: 'Beyond the Reach of US Law'

In a 118-page letter to the court dated June 24, Adani's lawyers at Sullivan & Cromwell laid out what they called "fatal weaknesses" in the government's case:

The transactions at issue were conducted by non-US entities, governed by English law, and structured entirely outside the United States — placing them beyond the scope of US securities law under the Supreme Court's Morrison ruling, the defence argued.

The alleged bribes were, according to an expert witness who is a former senior Indian regulatory official, actually transparent price reductions that Adani Green offered to state power companies to incentivise them to sign solar energy contracts — "ordinary commercial concessions, not bribes."

No investor lost money. The 2021 bond offering matured with all interest paid. The 2024 bonds have not missed a payment. The 2021 loan was repaid in full. The 2023 loan is not in default.

The Adani Group separately agreed to pay $275 million to the US Treasury Department to settle alleged violations of Iran sanctions, and a civil settlement with the SEC would see Adani and his nephew Sagar Adani pay $6 million and $12 million, respectively.

## What the Judge's Order Actually Means

Legal experts say this is standard procedure rather than a signal that the case will be revived. Under Rule 48(a) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, the government needs court approval to dismiss an indictment — and judges routinely ask for more information before granting that approval.

The precedent most observers are watching is the recent case of New York City Mayor Eric Adams, where a judge sought detailed explanations from prosecutors before ultimately allowing them to drop charges. The judiciary's authority to override a prosecutor's decision to abandon a case remains "extremely limited," legal analysts say.

But until Garaufis formally signs off, the charges remain officially pending — an overhang that has dogged the Adani Group for 18 months and one that investors and partners continue to watch.

## Why NRIs Should Care

The Adani Group is one of India's largest conglomerates, with interests spanning ports, airports, energy, cement, and data centres. Its stock prices, credit ratings, and ability to raise capital abroad are all directly affected by the legal cloud in the US. For NRIs with exposure to Indian markets — through direct holdings, index funds, or infrastructure bonds — the resolution of this case has real portfolio implications. The July 13 deadline will be the next moment to watch.
